messages.content: What is the largest planet in the universe?

function.name: space_star_info

message.content:
The largest planet that has been confirmed so far is **HD 100546 b**.  
It is a gas‑giant exoplanet orbiting the young star HD 100546, located about 320 light‑years away in the constellation Musca.  Its radius is roughly **2.5 times that of Jupiter**, making it the biggest planet we have directly imaged and measured.

> **Key facts about HD 100546 b**  
> • **Radius:** ≈ 2.5 R_Jupiter  
> • **Mass:** ≈ 10–20 M_Jupiter (estimates vary)  
> • **Orbit:** ~10 AU from its host star  
> • **Age:** ~5–10 million years (very young)

### Why it’s the largest known

- **Direct imaging**: Unlike most exoplanets, HD 100546 b was observed directly with high‑contrast imaging, allowing astronomers to estimate its size accurately.
- **Size comparison**: No other confirmed exoplanet has a radius larger than about 2.5 R_Jupiter.  
- **Brown dwarf boundary**: Planets larger than ~13 M_Jupiter may cross into the brown dwarf regime, but HD 100546 b’s mass is still below that threshold.

### Caveats

- **Observational limits**: We can only measure planets that are bright enough or close enough to their stars to be detected. There could be larger planets out there that we haven’t found yet.
- **Definition of “planet”**: Some very massive objects (brown dwarfs) blur the line between planets and stars. HD 100546 b sits comfortably within the planetary mass range.

So, as of now, HD 100546 b holds the title for the largest confirmed planet in the universe.
